# Mayhakajātaka (Ja 390)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mayhakajātaka* (Ja 390; PTS Jātaka iii. 299–302) is a birth story in the Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1883; Rhys Davids 1917]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha relates the story while dwelling at Jetavana regarding a wealthy "stranger merchant" (*āgantukaseṭṭhi*) in Sāvatthī who neither enjoyed his immense fortune himself nor gave it to others [Fausböll 1883]. In the story of the past, a man kills his brother's son out of greed for property [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. The Bodhisatta, appearing as the elder brother, admonishes him with stanzas opening with *Sakuṇo Mayhako nāma* ("There is a bird named Mayhaka") [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. The verses employ the simile of the mountain-dwelling Mayhaka bird that perches on a fig tree crying plaintively "Mine! Mine!" (*mayhaṁ mayhaṁ*) while flocks of other birds eat its ripe fruit, comparing it to a selfish person whose hoarded wealth brings no personal benefit and is consumed or seized by others [Anandajoti 2010; Cowell 1897; Fausböll 1883]. At the conclusion of the discourse, the Buddha identifies the miserly stranger merchant as the younger brother and himself as the elder brother [Fausböll 1883].

Scholars and commentators note that this narrative expands upon themes found in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* concerning deceased, childless misers who accumulated riches without distributing them, which also involve karmic accounts of almsgiving to the paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī [Rhys Davids 1917; Bodhi 2003; Jennings 1948]. Bhikkhu Bodhi further notes a partly parallel episode of abuse towards the paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī at Udāna 50 [Bodhi 2003]. In machine-computed text reuse, DharmaNexus identifies four matching passages between the text and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Tatiyo bhāgo), with no cross-language matches recorded with a similarity score of 10 or above [DharmaNexus].
